name: Black Hole Fireworks, the Tunnelling of a Black Hole into a White Hole
description: A shell of light falls in, makes a black hole, and after a long time comes back out of a white hole, in one spacetime with no event horizon and no singularity. Outside a finite region around the bounce the metric is an exact solution of Einstein's equations, flat inside the shell and Schwarzschild's outside it, glued to its own time reverse. Hal Haggard and Carlo Rovelli built it in 2014, and Carlos Barceló, Raúl Carballo-Rubio, and Luis Garay proposed a bounce of the same shape with a short wait.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ is the Schwarzschild radius of the shell of mass $M$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: In Hal M. Haggard and Carlo Rovelli's comparison, a ball dropped on a hard floor falls, bounces, and climbs back up the way it came, and with friction left out the film of it looks the same run backwards [haggard2015fireworks]. Could a collapsing star bounce the same way? In Einstein's theory it cannot, since a star that has fallen inside its Schwarzschild radius never comes out again [haggard2015fireworks]. Inside that radius Birkhoff's theorem allows the vacuum to be of either kind, "contracting towards a singularity (black-hole district) or expanding from a singularity (white-hole district)" [barcelo2014mutiny]. A star that bounces would have to go from the first district into the second [barcelo2014mutiny].¶A quantum version of the bounce was already known: in Petr Hájíček and Claus Kiefer's exact quantum theory of a thin shell of light, from 2001, the shell falls in and comes back out [hajicek2001shells]. "No absolute event horizon can form", they wrote, and the horizon itself turns "grey", a superposition of a black hole's and a white hole's [hajicek2001shells]. In Granada and Madrid, Carlos Barceló, Luis J. Garay, and Gil Jannes drew the spacetime of a shell that collapses and bounces, with gravity switched off near the Planck scale and the whole process over in less than a second [barcelo2011nongravity]. Early in 2014 Rovelli and Francesca Vidotto proposed that a collapsing star stops at the Planck density, held up by a quantum pressure as the universe of loop quantum cosmology is, and called it a Planck star [rovelli2014planck]. That stage is "very short in the star proper time" but "extremely long seen from the outside", since time runs so slowly beside the horizon [rovelli2014planck].¶The metric came that summer, in a preprint that Haggard and Rovelli posted on the 3rd of July, 2014, and dated, in the paper itself, the Fourth of July [haggard2015fireworks]. A thin shell of light falls in from far away, space inside it is flat, and outside it lies a piece of Martin D. Kruskal's extension of Schwarzschild's black hole, glued to its own time reverse [haggard2015fireworks, kruskal1960]. Einstein's equations hold everywhere except in a finite region around the place where the shell would have met its singularity, and that region reaches a little way outside the horizon [haggard2015fireworks]. Outside the shell the geometry is Schwarzschild's, but it covers part of Kruskal's spacetime twice, "a portion of a double cover" in their words: two overlapping flaps, opened up with the quantum region between them [haggard2015fireworks]. Nowhere is there an event horizon, and the causal structure is Minkowski's, with one trapped region on the way in and another on the way out [haggard2015fireworks].¶Why should quantum gravity reach outside a horizon, where the curvature is small? Haggard and Rovelli's answer is time: a uranium atom is stable from one moment to the next and has still most likely decayed after 4.5 billion years, and small quantum effects outside a black hole can pile up in the same way [haggard2015fireworks]. By their estimate the quantum region first appears at $7/6$ of the Schwarzschild radius, after a time of the order of $m^2$ in Planck units for a star of mass $m$ [haggard2015fireworks]. That is long beside the time $m$ of a collapse and short beside the $m^3$ of Hawking's evaporation [haggard2015fireworks, rovelli2014planck]. From far away the star sinks toward its horizon and fades, "a dimming, frozen star that reemerges" after the long wait, while for the shell itself the bounce is over almost at once [haggard2015fireworks].¶On the 5th of July, two days after Haggard and Rovelli posted theirs, Barceló, Raúl Carballo-Rubio, and Garay posted an essay with a bounce of the same shape, dated the 28th of March [barcelo2014mutiny]. It won an honourable mention from the Gravity Research Foundation that year, as Hájíček and Kiefer's essay had in 2001 [barcelo2014mutiny, hajicek2001shells]. Their star is J. Robert Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder's ball of dust, and outside it they wrote an acoustic metric, the kind that carries sound through a moving fluid, in Painlevé-Gullstrand coordinates: its flow falls in at $v = -c\sqrt{r_s/r}$ before the bounce and flows out at the same speed after it [barcelo2014mutiny, barcelo2015lifetime, barcelo2005, oppenheimersnyder1939]. Their bounce is quick, and a collapsing neutron star would stay apparently frozen at its Schwarzschild radius "for just a few tenths of a millisecond before being expelled again" [barcelo2015lifetime]. The price is a deeper causality under Einstein's, with no horizons, along which a signal leaves the bounce "even though the light cones are pointing inwards" [barcelo2015lifetime]. With Jannes they set the two proposals side by side and found one logarithm, the delay of light reflected just outside a horizon, read by Haggard and Rovelli as a long wait and by themselves as a short one [barcelo2015lifetime].¶Tommaso De Lorenzo and Alejandro Perez found that a white hole horizon lasting that long is unstable, since the energy density of quantum fields diverges on it [delorenzo2016fireworks]. So they made the bounce lopsided, a black hole that lasts a time of order $m^2$ followed by an explosion shorter than $m\log m$ in Planck units [delorenzo2016fireworks]. Marios Christodoulou, Rovelli, Simone Speziale, and Ilya Vilensky computed, in a first approximation, the amplitude of loop quantum gravity for the tunnelling, whose square fixes the lifetime as a function of the mass [christodoulou2016tunnelling]. Two years later Eugenio Bianchi, Christodoulou, Fabio D'Ambrosio, Haggard, and Rovelli moved the tunnelling to the end of Hawking's evaporation, where it is no longer suppressed [bianchi2018remnants]. The remnant is a white hole of about the Planck mass with an enormous interior, which lets out what fell in over a time of at least $m^4$ [bianchi2018remnants].

related.text: The outside of the shell, used twice: a black hole flap before the bounce and its time reverse, a white hole flap, after it. Together the two flaps cover part of Kruskal's spacetime twice [haggard2015fireworks].

The inside of the shell, flat on both sides of the bounce. It fills the inside of the light cone of the bounce, the past half before the shell turns round and the future half after it [haggard2015fireworks].
Vaidya's shell of null dust falling into flat space is this spacetime before the bounce, outside the quantum region, and his shell going out is this spacetime after it.
The same collapse made of dust. Israel's shell falls in with flat space inside it and Schwarzschild's outside, as this shell of light does, and this one comes back out [haggard2015fireworks].

The star of Barceló, Carballo-Rubio, and Garay's version of the bounce. In their proposal Oppenheimer and Snyder's ball of dust reaches the Planck density, bounces, and climbs back out through a white hole [barcelo2014mutiny].

Another white hole that does not last for ever. Novikov's core waits behind its past horizon from the big bang, and here the white hole is the time reverse of the collapse that came before it [novikov1965, haggard2015fireworks].

Another end to a collapse with no singularity and no event horizon. Hayward's black hole forms and evaporates with a regular centre, and Haggard and Rovelli count it among the models behind theirs [hayward2006, haggard2015fireworks].

coordinates.name: Flat Interior
coordinates.convention: We use the null coordinates $(u, v, \theta, \phi)$ of flat space, $u = ct - r$ and $v = ct + r$, both lengths, with $r = (v - u)/2$ the distance from the centre and the bounce at $u = v = 0$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Kruskal Exterior
domains: V \ge V_0 \;\text{(outside the shell falling in)}

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the shell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for its mass $M$

Areal radius, a length, the solution of $\left(1 - r/r_s\right)e^{r/r_s} = UV$, with $\mathrm{W}$ the principal branch of Lambert's function, $\mathrm{W}(x)\,e^{\mathrm{W}(x)} = x$; its derivatives are $\partial_U r = -r_s^2\,V e^{-r/r_s}/r$ and $\partial_V r = -r_s^2\,U e^{-r/r_s}/r$

coordinates.convention: We use Kruskal's null coordinates $(U, V, \theta, \phi)$, numbers normalised so that the shell falls in along the light ray $V = V_0$ and the surface of time symmetry outside the quantum region is $U + V = 0$, with the areal radius $r$ a function of $UV$ and $\mathrm{W}$ Lambert's function. The flap after the bounce is the mirror image $(U, V) \to (-V, -U)$, where the shell goes out along $U = -V_0$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Schwarzschild Exterior

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the shell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for its mass $M$

coordinates.convention: We use Schwarzschild coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $t = 0$ on the surface of time symmetry, and $R(t)$ is the areal radius of the shell. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Painlevé-Gullstrand

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the shell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for its mass $M$

coordinates.convention: We use Painlevé-Gullstrand coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ before the bounce, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, the proper time of observers falling in from rest at infinity, and $R(t)$ is the areal radius of the shell. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Outgoing Painlevé-Gullstrand

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the shell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for its mass $M$

coordinates.convention: We use Painlevé-Gullstrand coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ after the bounce, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, the proper time of observers flying out to rest at infinity, and $R(t)$ is the areal radius of the shell. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Lemaître
domains: r \ge R \;\text{(outside the shell falling in)}

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the shell, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ for its mass $M$
Areal radius, a length; its derivatives are $\partial_\rho r = \sqrt{r_s/r}$ and $\partial_\tau r = -c\sqrt{r_s/r}$

coordinates.convention: We use Lemaître's coordinates $(\tau, \rho, \theta, \phi)$ before the bounce, with $\tau$ carrying dimensions of time, the proper time of observers falling in from rest at infinity, each of whom keeps its $\rho$, a length, and $R$ is the areal radius of the shell. We take components in the chart $x^0 = c\tau$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{\tau}$ means $d(c\tau)/d\lambda$.
